summary:
We developed a web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx sky survey into a picture flipbook. A user enters the coordinates of a patch of sky, or picks a target such as WISE 0855 or Barnard’s Star, and the tool plays the SPHEREx images of that patch in time order, either by hand or in a short video like loop. Objects that move, such as asteroids, comets, nearby stars and brown dwarfs, visibly shift between frames, so anyone can spot them without special training.
Behind the scenes, our server finds every SPHEREx exposure covering the position, downloads only small cutouts. Users can choose the field of view and detector, mark spots, add images and filter them, and generate a spectrum on the fly. Because it queries NASA’s archive live, new data releases appear automatically.
This matters because SPHEREx produces more data than any one person or program can examine. A simple, public tool lets citizen scientists help discover new objects.
details:
Our tool turns NASA’s SPHEREx sky survey into a flipbook. The user enters coordinates (or picks a preset target), and the tool plays the SPHEREx images of that patch in time order, like a short video, so moving objects shift visibly between frames. The user can choose the field of view and the detector, and can add detectors together to improve signal-to-noise. A pen tool lets users mark and annotate objects directly on the frames.

The tool builds a spectrum on the fly from all exposures across the detectors. It labels the spectrum with the wavelengths of molecular features such as water (H2O), so users can see which molecules might be present.

Behind this, a Python server queries NASA’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx image covering the position and downloads only small cutouts.

Caching. Downloading and processing the images from the archive is slow, so we cache them on disk. After the first request, a position loads quickly, and we pre-load the five challenge targets so they open almost instantly.

Benefits

  • Anyone can spot moving objects without astronomy training or special software.
  • Adding detectors together reveals fainter objects than a single detector shows.
  • Spectra and molecular labels let users see what an object is made of, not just where it is.
  • It queries the archive live, so new data releases appear without code changes.

Intended impact

SPHEREx will produce more data than any one person or program can examine. We want to make that data approachable enough for citizen scientists, students and the public to help find asteroids, comets, nearby stars and brown dwarfs, as volunteers already do in projects like Backyard Worlds.

Tools and technologies

  • Python, FastAPI and Uvicorn for the server.
  • Astropy, astroquery and reproject for reading the FITS images, handling sky coordinates, and aligning frames.
  • NumPy and Pillow for image processing and PNG encoding.
  • NASA/IPAC IRSA archive (TAP queries and the cutout service) as the data source.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web interface.
  • pytest for testing, GitHub for collaboration. (check out our GitHub repo! https://github.com/nilsu-exe/oh_deer)
  • No special hardware: everything ran on laptops and a cloud host.

Creativity!

  • The flipbook idea turns a dataset of thousands of FITS files into something anyone can watch.
  • Because SPHEREx sees each patch of sky at different wavelengths in different exposures, we use that as a feature: stacking detectors and building spectra from the very exposures that make up the flipbook.
  • The pen tool and molecular labels make exploration interactive.

Factors we considered

  • Speed: archive queries and downloads are slow, so we used cutouts instead of full images, parallel downloads, and caching.
  • Mixing wavelengths: brightness changes between exposures at different wavelengths could be mistaken for motion, so we group frames by detector.
  • Honest limits: our spectra are quick-look measurements, not calibrated photometry, and very fast movers need a larger field of view.
  • Accessibility: the tool is simple enough for beginners, and coordinates in the URL make it easy to share and embed.
